title: Difference between creation and birth
english: Verse 18: “Now the birth of Jesus took place in this way” (Matthew 1:18). Here the evangelist mentions “birth,” but at the beginning of the Gospel he mentions “creation.” For here he says, “Now the birth of Jesus Christ took place in this way,” while there he says, “The book of the creation of Jesus Christ” (Matthew 1:1). What, then, is the difference between “birth” and “creation,” and how are both applied to Christ?

Consider a spoken word. By its own nature it is intangible and invisible. But when it is written in a book and, so to speak, given a body, then it is both seen and touched. The same is true of the Word of God. Before he became flesh he was fleshless and bodiless, neither seen nor written according to his divinity. But because he became flesh, he is both seen and inscribed. For this reason, since he became flesh, there is also a book of his creation.

But the question here is not why he said “book” and not “vision” or “word.” The question is what “birth” is and what “creation” is. Creation and birth differ. Creation is the first formation by God. Birth is the succession of one generation from another that comes from the penalty of death because of transgression. And further, creation possesses what is incorruptible and sinless, while birth possesses what is passible and prone to sin.

title: Luke's preface and the four approved Gospels
english: [Fragment apparently misplaced or corruptly transmitted.] The Lord, then, received by nature the sinlessness that belongs to creation, but he did not receive incorruptibility. What he received from birth was the passible.

“Since many have attempted to set forth an account of the things that have been fully assured among us” (Luke 1:1). Since it was an enormous undertaking for a human being to write down the teaching and words of God, Luke rightly makes a defense in his preface.

Just as in the ancient people many proclaimed prophecy, but some of them were false prophets and some were true prophets, and there was a gift of discernment of spirits by which the true prophet and the false prophet were distinguished, so also now in the New Testament many wanted to write Gospels.
But the approved money-changers did not accept them all; rather, they selected some of them.
Perhaps the word “attempted” also carries a hidden accusation against those who came rashly and without grace to the writing of the Gospels.
For Matthew did not attempt; he wrote, moved by the Holy Spirit. Likewise Mark, and John in similar fashion, and Luke.
But those who composed the Gospel entitled “According to the Egyptians” and the one entitled “Of the Twelve”—they attempted.
And Basilides has already dared to compose a Gospel according to Basilides.
Many, then, attempted; but the Church of God approves only the four.
He did not say simply “believed” but “fully assured,” testifying to the unshakeable certainty of what is reported.
And he said “things,” refuting the heresy of those who say that what happened through the Savior happened only in appearance.
Just as those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the Word delivered them to us (Luke 1:2).
